paragraphs.text: “1 Now the word of the LORD came unto Jonah the son of Amittai, saying, 2 ‘Arise, go to Nineveh, that great city, and cry against it; for their wickedness is come up before me.’” [1-2].
And in the Septuagint: “the cry of their wickedness is come up before me.”

The call was unique of its kind, for he is the only prophet who was called to serve a Gentile city, not to prophesy its destruction but to call it to repentance, so that the divine wrath might not fall upon it. It was not possible for this prophet or for anyone else to accept such a call, not out of hatred for the Gentiles but out of love for his own people, as we said before, that the salvation of the Gentiles is accomplished with the fall of Israel, and the faith of the world through the unbelief of the old people (Rom 11:11). In any case, since Jonah could not accept the call with his human mind, he fled; but God, who saw the purity of his heart, used even his flight to accomplish His divine purposes toward the Gentiles.

In the Septuagint it says: “for the cry of their wickedness is come up before me.” If the holy life shines in its most perfect form in the Lord Christ, who does not cry, nor does anyone hear His voice in the streets (Mt 12:19), then the wicked life carries in the ears of God a cry or clamor that heaven does not accept and that its Creator does not find restful, revealing the loss of inner peace. The wicked Cain killed his brother Abel and kept his mouth silent about the matter, but the marks of his evil were crying out through the shed blood of his brother, as the Lord says: “The voice of thy brother's blood crieth unto me from the ground” (Gen 4:10), and as it was said of the evil of Sodom and Gomorrah: “The cry of Sodom and Gomorrah is great” (Gen 18:20).

Jonah, whose name means “dove,” was called to preach in Nineveh, the great city, the cry of whose wickedness rose to heaven, as though God wanted to shatter the cries of evil with the meekness of the dove, to heal the inflamed wounds with soft oil, and to quench fire with water!

If the world has turned into unceasing clamor and bitter cries of injustice, it is in need of the Church, or of the true believer, who has the dove's eyes (Song 1:15; 4:1). They are the eyes of the Lord Christ, who says: “Learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart” (Mt 11:29), the eyes of the Holy Spirit, the true Dove, that by meekness we may inherit the earth (Mt 5:5) on behalf of the Lord Christ, so that it becomes His Kingdom, filled with joy and peace.

If the wicked are earth and not heaven because of their love of earthly things and their attachment to temporal things, then, since we carry within us the true Jonah, we win them by the meekness of His Holy Spirit, so that they no longer remain earth but become heaven. As St. John Climacus says: [The Lord finds rest in meek hearts, but the troubled spirit is the seat of Satan. The meek inherit the earth, or rather they rule over it, but those of evil character are driven from their land].

If Nineveh, the great city, represents the body, the cries of whose evil desires rise before the Lord, then no one is able to remove these cries from it except our true Jonah, who fills the soul and sanctifies the body as well.

“But Jonah rose up to flee unto Tarshish from the presence of the LORD, and went down to Joppa; and he found a ship going to Tarshish: so he paid the fare thereof, and went down into it, to go with them unto Tarshish from the presence of the LORD” [3].
Why did Jonah want to flee to Tarshish from the presence of the Lord instead of going to Nineveh?

First: St. Jerome holds that Jonah could not bear to go to Nineveh and have it saved at the expense of his own people Israel, so he disobeyed the Lord not out of hatred in his heart but out of zeal for his people, as though he were imitating the zealous prophet Moses in his saying: “Yet now, if thou wilt forgive their sin; and if not, blot me, I pray thee, out of thy book which thou hast written” (Ex 32:32). Moses appeared as one who resisted the Lord, yet he obtained God's mercies for his people, and God did not blot out his name from His book. In the same spirit the Apostle Paul says: “For I could wish that myself were accursed from Christ for my brethren, my kinsmen according to the flesh: who are Israelites” (Rom 9:3). He desired that he himself be cut off so that his brethren might live in Christ, counting his death a gain; by this love he did not die but deserved the life he desired for them. So Jonah feared that his preaching to the Assyrians, the enemies of Israel, would mean the destruction of Israel itself, and he fled to Tarshish, that is, in the opposite direction. Some think it is Tartessus, in southern Spain near Gibraltar, or Carthage in North Africa.

Second: The word “Tarshish,” as St. Jerome sees it, means “sea” or “contemplation in joy.” If the word “Joppa” in Canaanite means “beauty,” then Jonah, instead of setting out by God's commandment to preach salvation to Nineveh, preferred to go down to the beauty of his human thought and human wisdom, that is, to Joppa, to cast himself into Tarshish, that is, into the sea of this world or into joyful contemplations, without true striving and without actually carrying the Cross. This behavior represents the conduct of the man who walks according to his own desire and not according to the Lord's difficult commandment.

Third: The prophet Jonah, while knowing that God is “the God of heaven, which hath made the sea and the dry land” (Jon 1:9), and even bearing witness to it, rushes to flee from God when he leans on his human thought apart from faith. As St. John Chrysostom says: [Truly he fled from the land, but he did not flee from the wrath of God! He fled from the earth, but he brought storms upon himself in the sea]. It would have been fitting for him rather not to flee from God but to God, for in Him alone the believer finds his peace and safety!

4 But the LORD sent out a great wind into the sea, and there was a mighty tempest in the sea, so that the ship was like to be broken. 5 Then the mariners were afraid, and cried every man unto his god, and cast forth the wares that were in the ship into the sea, to lighten it of them. But Jonah was gone down into the sides of the ship; and he lay, and was fast asleep. 6 So the shipmaster came to him, and said unto him, “What meanest thou, O sleeper? arise, call upon thy God, if so be that God will think upon us, that we perish not.” 7 And they said every one to his fellow, “Come, and let us cast lots, that we may know for whose cause this evil is upon us.” So they cast lots, and the lot fell upon Jonah.

If Jonah fled to the sea from the Maker of the sea Himself, the Lord therefore summoned him in a new language fitting for him as a fugitive, the language of successive afflictions, for “the LORD sent out a great wind into the sea, and there was a mighty tempest in the sea, so that the ship was like to be broken” [4]. The Lord began to speak to him in the language of the great wind, the mighty tempest and the ship that had lost its balance, things that suit Jonah and reveal what was within him: a wind of violent disobedience, a great tempest of inner turmoil, and the unbalanced ship of his heart.

St. Jerome says: [Jonah's flight points to the condition of man in general, for by despising the commandments of the Lord he fled from His face and gave himself over to the world, and the tempest of the world grew fierce upon him until he was about to drown; then he was compelled to contemplate God and to return to the One from whom he had fled... The ship was in danger... and the waves were stirred up by the winds... for when the Lord is not pleased, nothing is safe].

The strangers heard the voice of God, though they did not know Him, while the ears of Jonah grew heavy to hear, for it says: “Then the mariners were afraid, and cried every man unto his god, and cast forth the wares that were in the ship into the sea, to lighten it of them. But Jonah was gone down into the sides of the ship; and he lay, and was fast asleep” [4-5]. The mariners were pagans, and their knowledge of God was mixed with much error, and yet when God spoke in the language of hardship and affliction they were filled with fear and did nothing until each one of them cried out to his god; so God, for them, came first and before everything else, although they did not know Him.

St. Jerome says: [They thought the ship was too heavy with its natural cargo, and did not realize that the weight was due to the fugitive prophet. The mariners were afraid, and each one cried out to his god, for they were ignorant of the truth, yet they were not ignorant of divine providence. Through their mistaken religion they knew something and perceived some spiritual depth... But as for Israel, neither prosperity nor pain could lead it to the knowledge of God. Therefore Joshua wept much over the people, while the eyes of the people were dry].

The pagans were crying out to their gods and throwing their cargo into the sea, each one praying and working as much as he could, but Jonah, though he knew that he was the cause of the calamity, went down into the sides of the ship to sleep a heavy sleep, as though he did not want to see the waves of God's wrath against him, or like one who took a narcotic to flee from his painful reality.

If Jonah's sleep represents a kind of slackness, yet at the same time it gave us a good prophetic aspect. On the one hand, he represented humanity at rest in the Lord amid the waves of this troubled world. When Herod was about to bring out the Apostle Peter to kill him (Acts 12:6), Peter was sleeping soundly, bound with two chains between two soldiers in prison and under strict guard. On the other hand, Jonah represented the Lord Christ, who slept on the Cross as in the ship, to raise up the new Eve from His pierced side, enjoying true rest in Him; He also slept on the Cross so as to be buried in the belly of the earth and rise, granting us the power of the Resurrection. As St. Jerome says: [While the others were in danger, he was safe, sleeping and rising. And at his request, and by the mystery of his sufferings, he saved those who awakened him].

Let us return to the mariners and their shipmaster, and we find them acting with surpassing wisdom together with gentleness and meekness, for it says: “So the shipmaster came to him, and said unto him, What meanest thou, O sleeper? arise, call upon thy God, if so be that God will think upon us, that we perish not. And they said every one to his fellow, Come, and let us cast lots, that we may know for whose cause this evil is upon us. So they cast lots, and the lot fell upon Jonah” [6-7].

The shipmaster was marked by surpassing meekness in his speech to the prophet, who was sleeping soundly at a time when everyone was crying out and praying and throwing the cargo into the sea... He spoke with exceeding gentleness in which he did not wound his feelings, and urged him to pray kindly, something we sometimes do not find in believers, and even in shepherds themselves, who lose their peace when rebuking and lose their calm while setting others right.

We say that God, who had earlier spoken with the prophet, perhaps through a vision or a revelation concerning the work in Nineveh, came back to speak to him through raging nature, and since he had stopped his ears, He spoke to him through the pagans, saying to him: “What meanest thou, O sleeper? arise, call upon thy God, if so be that God will think upon us, that we perish not.” As though He were saying: “Why are you sleeping inside your heart? Your God from whom you flee is able to save us Gentiles from perishing. If you love your people and your nation, listen to our supplications, look upon our longing, and do not despise our faith. Even if we do not yet know the God whom you worship, by faith we accept Him, so let us not perish!”

Remarkably, the sailors cast lots, and God revealed the truth, and they realized that Jonah was the cause of God's wrath... As St. Jerome says: [If God guided them through the lot, He is only speaking to them through their own thinking, and this does not justify our use of lots. God guided Balaam through his ass (Num 22:28), to show him that the dumb beast perceived what man in his wickedness did not perceive, and as God spoke with the Magi through the star, and as He allowed Caiaphas to prophesy without knowing it when he said that one man should die for all the people. In any case, if Jonah in his love for his people made light of the salvation of the Gentiles, God revealed to him through the lot that He does not despise a Gentile, but speaks to them in their own language and reveals the truth to them even through their own practice; so what the lot presented carried a hidden divine rebuke to Jonah, who made light of the salvation of the Gentiles!].

8 Then said they unto him, “Tell us, we pray thee, for whose cause this evil is upon us; What is thine occupation? and whence comest thou? what is thy country? and of what people art thou?” 9 And he said unto them, “I am an Hebrew; and I fear the LORD, the God of heaven, which hath made the sea and the dry land.” 10 Then were the men exceedingly afraid, and said unto him, “Why hast thou done this?” For the men knew that he fled from the presence of the LORD, because he had told them. 11 Then said they unto him, “What shall we do unto thee, that the sea may be calm unto us?” for the sea wrought, and was tempestuous. 12 And he said unto them, “Take me up, and cast me forth into the sea; so shall the sea be calm unto you: for I know that for my sake this great tempest is upon you.”

“Then said they unto him, Tell us, we pray thee, for whose cause this evil is upon us; What is thine occupation? and whence comest thou? what is thy country? and of what people art thou? And he said unto them, I am an Hebrew; and I fear the LORD, the God of heaven, which hath made the sea and the dry land” [8-9].

In the midst of the violent currents, the mighty tempest and the surrounding danger, we would have expected the mariners to lose their peace and calm, but they proved to be wise; since they saw a mystery in Jonah, they began to ask him about his whole life in detail... seeking true knowledge. Their questions were a gentle rebuke that God used to set Jonah himself right, for while they were asking, it was fitting for Jonah to examine himself about his conduct. As St. Jerome said: [The purpose of the lot was that the mariners would press him to confess with his own tongue the cause of this tempest and the reason for God's wrath]. That is, to confess his disobedience to the Lord and his flight from the One who made the sea and the dry land.

The questions brought the desired result, for he confessed, saying: “I am an Hebrew; and I fear the LORD, the God of heaven, which hath made the sea and the dry land.” As St. Jerome says: [He did not say “I am an Hebrew” meaning the title proper to his people, belonging to one of its tribes, but he meant that he is a passer-by like Abraham, as though saying: I am weak and a wayfarer like all my fathers, as it says in the Psalm: “They went from one city to another and from one kingdom to another people...” I fear the Lord, the God of heaven, and not the gods to whom you pray, which are unable to save. I pray to the God of heaven, who made the sea and the dry land, the sea to which I flee, and the land from which I flee!].

Jonah confessed his fault, and the mariners came to know the truly fearful God, for it says: “Then were the men exceedingly afraid, and said unto him, Why hast thou done this? For the men knew that he fled from the presence of the LORD, because he had told them” [10]. They understood that he was a holy man fleeing from the holy God, so they asked him not to rebuke him but, as St. Jerome says: [inquiring about the mystery of his conduct].
After enjoying the knowledge of God they asked Jonah: “What shall we do unto thee, that the sea may be calm unto us? for the sea wrought, and was tempestuous” [11].

St. Jerome says: [As though they were saying: You say that because of you the wind, the waves and the sea are in turmoil. You have revealed to us the cause of the sickness, so disclose the remedy. Behold, the sea rises against us, and we know that we have become the object of wrath because we took you. We erred in receiving you as a guest, so what shall we do that the wrath of God may be calmed toward us? What shall we do to you? Shall we kill you? But you are of those who believe in the Lord! Shall we keep you? You are fleeing from God! Now we have nothing but to carry out your command, so command us, that the sea may be calm, for its turmoil bears witness to the wrath of the Creator... There can be no more delay before the vengeance of the Creator?].
“And he said unto them, Take me up, and cast me forth into the sea; so shall the sea be calm unto you: for I know that for my sake this great tempest is upon you” [12].

Jonah offered the remedy, which was to cast him into the raging sea so that the great tempest might be calm, for the tempest was because of his disobedience to the Lord and would not calm except by throwing him into the waters for his repentance; and on the other hand, Jonah, as a representative of the Lord Christ, who bore the sins of the world, had to be cast upon the Cross and delivered to the tomb, that the believers in Him might enjoy reconciliation with the Father and enter into His eternal peace.

St. John Chrysostom says: [Jonah expected to flee by means of the ship, but the ship became chains to him]. He thought he could flee from the God of the sea by means of a ship, but God seized him amid the raging waters inside the ship, to confine him in distress and bring him to repentance. God used the very means that Jonah thought was his escape from the hand of God in order to seize him and bring him back to Himself. How beautiful is the statement of St. John Chrysostom: [There was no need for many days or for continual counsels, but simply put, there was need that everything lead him to repentance (that is, God uses all circumstances for his salvation). For God did not lead him from the ship directly to the city, but the mariners handed him over to the sea, and the sea to the whale, and the whale to God, and God to the people of Nineveh, and through this long circuit He brought back the wanderer, so that all might know that it is not possible to flee from the hand of God].

St. Jerome comments on the words Jonah spoke to the mariners, saying: [This tempest is seeking me; it threatens you with drowning so that you may seize me, and by my death you will live! I know in truth that this great tempest is because of me... Behold, the waves command you to cast me into the sea, and you will find calm... Let us notice here the greatness of the fugitive: he does not evade, nor conceal the matter, nor deny it after confessing his flight from God, but accepts the punishment with a wide heart. He wants to die so that others may not be destroyed because of him].

St. Jerome also has a beautiful comment on these words of Jonah as a prophecy about the work of the Lord Christ, our true Jonah, who accepted to die to redeem all the people, saying: [Our Jonah says: I know in truth that for my sake this great tempest is upon you; for since the winds see me sailing with you to Tarshish, that is, to “joyful contemplation,” I lead you to glory, so that where I am, there you may be also with the Father; therefore wrath occurs. The world weeps and nature is troubled! Death wants to swallow me so as to kill you at the same time, not realizing that it takes me as bait, for by my death it dies! Take me, then, and cast me into the sea!]

entries.section: 5. Jonah in the belly of the fish:

paragraphs.text: 13 Nevertheless the men rowed hard to bring it to the land; but they could not: for the sea wrought, and was tempestuous against them. 14 Wherefore they cried unto the LORD, and said, “We beseech thee, O LORD, we beseech thee, let us not perish for this man's life, and lay not upon us innocent blood: for thou, O LORD, hast done as it pleased thee.” 15 So they took up Jonah, and cast him forth into the sea: and the sea ceased from her raging. 16 Then the men feared the LORD exceedingly, and offered a sacrifice unto the LORD, and made vows. 17 Now the LORD had prepared a great fish to swallow up Jonah. And Jonah was in the belly of the fish three days and three nights.

“Nevertheless the men rowed hard to bring it to the land; but they could not: for the sea wrought, and was tempestuous against them. Wherefore they cried unto the LORD, and said, We beseech thee, O LORD, we beseech thee, let us not perish for this man's life, and lay not upon us innocent blood: for thou, O LORD, hast done as it pleased thee” [13-14].

This book brings out in simplicity the good aspects of these Gentiles. At the beginning they did not throw their cargo overboard, nor act according to their experience as sailors, until each one had cried out to his god; so they put their gods first, before their experience, something many believers ignore. Again, when they cast lots and the lot fell on Jonah, they did not wound his feelings with a word nor insult him, despite the many losses that came upon them because of him; and even when he confessed his fault and pointed them to throw him into the sea, they tried to save him by every means, and when they failed completely and realized that it was God's will that they cast him into the sea, they were trembling, fearing the wrath of God, and asking Him not to let them perish for the life of this man! Were not these actions, full of love, gentleness and wisdom, enough to rebuke Jonah, whom the Lord called for the salvation of the Gentiles in Nineveh, yet he fled! It presented to him a sample of Gentiles who surpass the believers themselves. If they were compared with the Jews, who had the Law and the prophecies with them and saw the wonderful works of Christ and the witness of heaven and earth and the sea and all His creation; even Pilate the Gentile washed his hands before them, and yet they cried “His blood be on us, and on our children,” are they not counted better than they?!
St. Jerome comments on the actions of the mariners, saying:

[They wanted to draw the oar and defeat nature so as not to disgrace the prophet of the Lord... They thought they were able to save the ship from danger, and did not take into account the role Jonah had to play, that he must suffer].

[Great was the faith of the mariners, for they were in danger and yet were praying for the life of another. They knew well that spiritual death is more dreadful than natural death, for they said: “lay not upon us innocent blood.” They make God Himself a witness, so that He would not accuse them of what they could not prevent, as though they were saying to Him: We do not want to kill Your prophet; rather he declared Your wrath against him, and the tempest confirmed Your will, O Lord, which we are carrying out with our hands].

[While the Gentiles did not want the death of Christ, affirming that it was innocent blood (Mt 27:25), the Jews say: “His blood be on us, and on our children”; therefore when they lift their hands toward heaven they are not answered, because their hands are full of blood].

entries.section: 5. Jonah in the belly of the fish:

paragraphs.text: “So they took up Jonah, and cast him forth into the sea: and the sea ceased from her raging” [15].

St. Jerome says: [It does not say “they seized him” or “they fell upon him,” but “they took him up,” as those who carried him with respect and honor, and cast him into the sea, he having given himself into their hands without resistance; then the sea ceased from its raging, for it found the one it was seeking. When we follow the trail of a fugitive we run after him with all the power of our feet, and when we seize him we stop with the prize. So the sea was raging without Jonah, and when the one it desired was taken into its depths, it rejoiced at taking him, kept festival for him, and grew calm with joy].

St. John Chrysostom sees in the casting of the disobedient Jonah into the sea an indication of the expulsion of sin from the ship of our life, that our true peace, which our iniquities took away, may return to us, for he says: [The city was troubled because of the sins of the people of Nineveh, and the ship was troubled because of the prophet's disobedience. Therefore the mariners cast Jonah into the deep, and the ship was preserved. Let us also cast out our sins, and our city will remain in sure safety!].

St. Jerome sees in the casting of Jonah into the sea an indication of the sufferings of the Lord Christ, which removed the raging of our sea and saved the ship and those in it from danger. Through the sufferings of the Lord Christ the world was filled with surpassing inner peace!

entries.section: 5. Jonah in the belly of the fish:

paragraphs.text: “Then the men feared the LORD exceedingly, and offered a sacrifice unto the LORD, and made vows” [16].

When Jonah was cast into the sea, that is, when the Lord Christ bore sufferings unto death, He saved us from the old pagan worship, granting us His great fear, the offering of His unique propitiatory sacrifice, and the fulfillment of our vows to the Lord, that is, the complete consecration of our life to Him.

St. Jerome says: [When the fugitive Jonah died in the sea, the ship that was shaken by the winds was saved, and the idolaters were saved]. He also says: [Before the sufferings of the Lord they prayed to their gods under the influence of fear (Jon 1:10), but after the sufferings they feared Him, that is, they worshiped and glorified Him... They feared Him exceedingly, that is, with all the soul and all the heart and all the mind (Deut 6:5; Mt 22:37). And they offered a sacrifice; certainly this does not mean the literal sense, for there are no sacrifices in the sea, but the sacrifice of the Lord is the genuine spirit, as it is said: “Offer unto the Lord the sacrifice of praise; and pay thy vows unto the most High” (Ps 49:14)]...

Therefore by the casting of Jonah into the sea, or the Lord Christ's entering into His sufferings, the spirit of the fear of God came upon us, and we gained the right to offer His holy sacrifice and to fulfill our vows to Him!
“Now the LORD had prepared a great fish to swallow up Jonah. And Jonah was in the belly of the fish three days and three nights” [7].

Things did not proceed without divine ordering or planning, but God, who sent the great wind so that a mighty tempest arose declaring God's wrath against disobedience, is the One who sent a huge fish beside the ship to swallow Jonah, to give him a safe lodging and not death, revealing to him God's care for him. St. Jerome says: [The Lord showed His wrath when Jonah was in the ship, and showed His joy when he entered into death], explaining that this is because he represents the Lord Christ, who put death to death by His death. Truly Jonah appeared as a victim of death swallowed by hell, but it could not hold him within more than three days and three nights, but cast him out of its belly, so that the prophet might say: “O death, where are thy plagues? O Hades, where is thy sting?” (Hos 13:14).

The Lord Christ affirmed what happened to Jonah in the belly of the fish as a type of what happened to the Lord Himself, by saying: “For as Jonah was three days and three nights in the whale's belly; so shall the Son of man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth” (Mt 12:40).
How did the Lord Christ remain in the earth for this period?

First: St. Jerome holds that the Jews count part of a day as a whole day, so the period of the Lord Christ's death is counted from Friday to Sunday, although He died at the end of Friday and rose at dawn on Sunday. St. John Chrysostom holds that if the Lord had remained until the end of Sunday, the soldiers would have left the tomb, and the Jews would have believed that the news of the Resurrection was the work of the disciples, fabricated after the soldiers left the site; therefore He rose while the soldiers were guarding the tomb.
Second: St. Jerome presents an opinion held by some, which is to consider the hours of darkness on the Cross as a new night, unique of its kind.

Third: Some count the period of burial from the moment the Lord delivered His broken Body into the bowels of His disciples at the Last Supper, as one buried in the human earth to raise it with Him as a heaven for Himself by His Resurrection at dawn on Sunday.

In any case, the Lord was buried three days and rose; this is the truth to which the disciples bore witness and which the Lord confirmed with many proofs, that we might live it as the mystery of our daily resurrection and our victory over death and hell.
Moreover, Jonah, by his entering into death and coming out, was used as a living proof of the resurrection of the body on the last day.

entries.section: 1. His prayer in the belly of the fish:

paragraphs.text: 1 Then Jonah prayed unto the LORD his God out of the fish's belly. Who among us can express the distress into which Jonah entered?! In the belly of the fish Jonah descended into affliction as into a tomb, in which his own thoughts, abilities and resources died; he did not know what to do, nor could he foresee what would befall him. The fish would float on the waters, and Jonah would breathe air and see a glimmer of light; it would take him down into the waters, and he would find himself in pitch darkness. The fish would open its mouth, and Jonah would be drowned in salt water; the fish would expel the water, and Jonah would recover his breath. So Jonah lived a few days; were it not for God's care for him and His favors toward him, every second of them would have been a heavy mountain crushing his soul, and death would have become for him a desire.

In any case, in his affliction Jonah was joined to the Lord buried in the tomb, through type and shadow, and so he set out with his heart and mind not to the outside of the fish but to what is above the place; he rose up to God praying as one in a heavenly sanctuary, for it says: “Then Jonah prayed unto the LORD his God out of the fish's belly” [1].

Before, he called the Lord “the God of heaven” (Jon 1:9), but in affliction it says “the LORD his God”... The Lord is attributed to Jonah as his God. He is the God of the afflicted and the suffering, as though He leaves His heavens and comes down to Jonah to support him in his distress, or, in other words, He turns his life into a heaven in which the Lord his God dwells, so He is called his God, that is, the God of the heavens in which He dwells. Our God is the God of Jonah the sufferer who carries the Cross, the God of every embittered soul; He enters him so that he may be called “the God of heaven”... for He makes of those who carry the Cross holy heavens.

Jonah gave us his wonderful prayer, indeed his unique prophetic hymn, not in moments of ease, nor inside the temple building as a teacher, but in the midst of sufferings as one in the tomb of the crucified Lord Christ. As St. John Chrysostom says: [Let us not be concerned with the place but with the Lord of the place, for Jonah was in the belly of the fish and the Lord listened to his prayer. And you, even if you are in the baths, pray. Wherever you are, pray; do not seek a place in which to pray, for your soul is a temple].

If the Church is concerned even with the building, that it may be an icon of heaven, it is so that we may bear the marks of heaven in us, and look to the inner spiritual building, and our eyes may be lifted to the holy things that the Holy Spirit establishes in us, especially in moments of affliction and pain!

Affliction is the Golgotha in which we enjoy being crucified with our Lord Jesus, that we may go forth with Him to His glories and be with Him and in Him in the bosom of the heavenly Father by His Holy Spirit.

2 And said, “I cried by reason of mine affliction unto the LORD, and he heard me; out of the belly of hell cried I, and thou heardest my voice. 3 For thou hadst cast me into the deep, in the midst of the seas; and the floods compassed me about: all thy billows and thy waves passed over me. 4 Then I said, I am cast out of thy sight; yet I will look again toward thy holy temple. 5 The waters compassed me about, even to the soul: the depth closed me round about, the weeds were wrapped about my head. 6 I went down to the bottoms of the mountains; the earth with her bars was about me for ever: yet hast thou brought up my life from corruption, O LORD my God. 7 When my soul fainted within me I remembered the LORD: and my prayer came in unto thee, into thine holy temple.
“I cried by reason of mine affliction unto the LORD, and he heard me; out of the belly of hell cried I, and thou heardest my voice” [2].

When Jonah was cast into the salt waters he entered the belly of the fish, not to see death with his eyes but to behold, through the shadow, the Lord Christ Himself cast into affliction with us and for us, so that when He cries out with His blameless life the Father answers Him and lifts us with Him above affliction. The One who is without blemish came down to our lowliness that we might become in Him the object of the Father's pleasure, that He might hear us in our affliction and lift us up to Himself. As St. Jerome says: [The Lord came down; for our sake He humbled Himself, that we might ascend in safety and confidence].

Jonah called on the Lord in his affliction and enjoyed the answer at once, for he saw himself ascending not from the belly of the fish but from the belly of hell in Christ Jesus crucified! Here he speaks in the past tense, not the future: “he heard me,” “thou heardest my voice,” the form of true enjoyment through the type, and the form of certainty that carries no doubt.

The prophet Jeremiah bore the same feelings and grasped the same concepts when he was cast into the pit, for he said: “I called upon thy name, O LORD, out of the low dungeon. Thou hast heard my voice: hide not thine ear at my breathing, at my cry” (Lam 3:55-56).
“For thou hadst cast me into the deep, in the midst of the seas; and the floods compassed me about” [3].

Jonah realized that it was God who cast him into the deep, in the midst of the seas, and not the mariners. But the wonder is that when he went down even to the depths he did not find himself under the weight of the pressure of the seas' waters and their dangers, but found himself surrounded by a holy river that waters him and gladdens him with abundant spiritual fruit, the river of which it is said in the Psalm: “There is a river, the streams whereof shall make glad the city of God” (Ps 46:4). In the midst of bitter affliction, “In the multitude of my thoughts within me thy comforts delight my soul”; instead of the bitter salt waters I have the sweet waters of the river, and instead of the weight of the waters upon me, the waters surround me for delight and joy.

What is the midst of the seas into which Jonah was cast? It is the depths of the bitter Cross, which the Lord Christ entered as a propitiatory sacrifice for the whole world, and through it He caused the sweet, life-giving waters of Baptism to burst forth, so that a river surrounded Him, that is, His Church, which is His Body: the river of Baptism, that is, the waters of the Jordan. This sight drew the hearts of the prophets, so the prophet Ezekiel says about the Church of the New Testament, or the new temple: “Afterward he brought me again unto the door of the house; and, behold, waters issued out from under the threshold of the house eastward... and the waters came down from under from the right side of the house, at the south side of the altar... a river that I could not pass over: for the waters were risen, waters to swim in, a river that could not be passed over... for they shall come thither, and they shall be healed; and every thing shall live whither the river cometh... And by the river upon the bank thereof, on this side and on that side, shall grow all trees for meat, whose leaf shall not fade, neither shall the fruit thereof be consumed: it shall bring forth new fruit according to his months, because their waters they issued out of the sanctuary: and the fruit thereof shall be for meat, and the leaf thereof for medicine” (Ezek 47).

Our sins cast the Lord Christ, in His love for us, into the midst of the seas, to bear the divine wrath for us through the Cross, turning the saltiness of the seas into the sweetness of rivers, so that He gives us in Him, through the Cross itself, the river of His Holy Spirit, who waters our souls and gives them fruit and grants them healing! Thus the Cross bore two complementary images: the image of God's wrath against sin, which cost the Lord His life, and the image of God's surpassing love, which caused the springs of His surpassing grace to burst forth.

St. Jerome says: [For the Savior the Lord, the image came in the Psalm: “I sink in deep mire, where there is no standing: I am come into deep waters, where the floods overflow me” (Ps 69:3), as it is said of Him in another Psalm: “But thou hast cast off and abhorred, thou hast been wroth with thine anointed. Thou hast made void the covenant of thy servant: thou hast profaned his crown by casting it to the ground. Thou hast broken down all his hedges” (Ps 89:39)... And although He was in salt waters, being tempted in all things, yet they were not salt (bitter) for Him, for a river surrounded Him, as it is said in another place: “There is a river, the streams whereof shall make glad the city of God” (Ps 46:4)].

St. Ambrose speaks to us of this river that surrounds us as the Holy Spirit, who waters the heavenly Jerusalem, who overflowed upon the Church through Christ Jesus crucified. [The Holy Spirit is the river, the plentiful river, the great river that flows always without ceasing... For the heavenly Jerusalem is not watered by an earthly river but by the Holy Spirit].

Through the Cross we have enjoyed the river of the New Testament instead of the well of the Old Testament. As St. Ambrose says: [The Old Testament is a deep well from which water is drawn with effort; it was not full to the brim, but there came after it the One who says: “I am not come to destroy (the Law), but to fulfil” (Mt 5:17)... But the New Testament is not merely a river, but “out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water” (Jn 7:38), rivers of understanding, rivers of contemplation, spiritual rivers]. Thus, when the Lord sits with us at the well, as with the Samaritan woman at noon, that is, in the moments of the Cross, He causes the springs of His waters to burst forth in us like living, gladdening rivers.

The prophet continues his hymn on the tongue of the Lord Christ, saying: “all thy billows and thy waves passed over me” [3]. St. Jerome comments on this phrase, saying: [Let us inquire how the billows and waves passed over the Savior... for there is no one able to endure all trials except the One who was tempted in all things... All the afflictions and toils that trouble the human race and that break all ships passed over His head... He endured the storm and all the turmoil so that others might be in calm!].

If the billows point to the judgments of God, as St. Cyril the Great says: [The Lord bore upon Himself all the judgments of God against us. All the judgments fell upon Him to be fulfilled in His body, as the Psalmist says: “Deep calleth unto deep at the noise of thy waterspouts: all thy waves and thy billows are gone over me” (Ps 42:7). Thus the Lord Christ appeared as the One who pays the debt, as one cast out from the eyes of the Father, although He is the Intercessor who carries His people into the heavenly sanctuaries. Therefore the prophet continues his speech: “Then I said, I am cast out of thy sight; yet I will look again toward thy holy temple” [4].

It is a realistic picture of the Cross: on one side the Savior appeared as one cast out, crying out and saying: “My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?” (Mt 27:46). On the other side, He bears humanity in His body that it may be glorified with Him. As St. Jerome says: [The Lord became as one in your position (cast out)... in order to lift humanity up to be with Him where He is (Jn 17:2)]. He carries out His work as the greatest High Priest, entering into the temple of His heavenly sanctuary, bearing His Church into the very heavenly places, as the Apostle says: “For Christ is not entered into the holy places made with hands, which are the figures of the true; but into heaven itself, now to appear in the presence of God for us” (Heb 9:24). So while He is cast out for our sake, He bears us in Him that we may be the object of the Father's good pleasure and delight.

Jonah was not a priest to enter the Holy Place, nor a high priest to enjoy the sight of the Holy of Holies once every year, but in the depths of the sea, when he became as one cast out, he was counted a type of the Lord Christ, who was cast out and entered His heavenly sanctuaries. As St. Jerome says: [In the depths of the sea he sees the temple of the Lord, and in the spirit of prophecy he found himself there contemplating something else].
“The waters compassed me about, even to the soul: the depth closed me round about... yet hast thou brought up my life from corruption, O LORD my God” [5-6].

The Lord Christ descended into hell and became as one whom the waters compassed about, even to the soul, but the waters could not swallow Him; rather He frees those whom the waters had taken captive and drowned. He descended into the depths of the waters so that those drowned in them might ascend with Him, as the Apostle says: “Now that he ascended, what is it but that he also descended first into the lower parts of the earth? He that descended is the same also that ascended up far above all heavens, that he might fill all things” (Eph 4:9-10).

St. Augustine sees in the waters that compassed the Lord Christ, even to the soul, an expression of what happened at the Cross, for everyone rose against Him like the waves of the sea, and in His humility He submitted willingly for our sake, saying: “I am come into deep waters, where the floods overflow me” (Ps 69:2). He did not resist the violent words nor the cruel actions, but endured them patiently, and “became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross” (Phil 2:8).

The Savior who walked on the waters (Mt 14:26) bent Himself down to the waters so that they would compass Him for a time and surround Him, that He might carry His believers over the waters through the ship of His Cross and bring them safely to the harbor of the heavenly Jerusalem.

Again he says: “When my soul fainted within me I remembered the LORD: and my prayer came in unto thee, into thine holy temple” [7]. Jonah lost all hope in a human arm for salvation, for he became as one seized in the belly of the fish, with no one to save him but the Lord; therefore he says: “I remembered the LORD.” It is as though he were with the Psalmist who says: “When my father and my mother forsake me, then the LORD will take me up.” As St. Jerome says: [I found myself shut up in the bowels of the fish, so all my hope became in the Lord].

This phrase also applies to our suffering Jonah, who cried out in the flesh: “My soul is exceeding sorrowful, even unto death” (Mt 26:38), “O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me” (Mt 26:39). This burden that the Lord bore for our sake was so that He might carry out His priestly work through His propitiatory sacrifice and ask the Father on our behalf: “My prayer came in unto thee, into thine holy temple.” As St. Jerome says: [As a priest He pleads for the deliverance of the people in His body].
“8 They that observe lying vanities forsake their own mercy. 9 But I will sacrifice unto thee with the voice of thanksgiving; I will pay that that I have vowed. Salvation is of the LORD.” [8-9].

At the Cross there appeared those who observe lying vanities, those who followed the vanities of the Pharisees and so were deprived of the Lord Himself, their “mercy.” They were deprived of Christ their Savior and became like a satanic hymn that proclaims nothing but words of falsehood and blasphemy. But the Lord Christ, who was slandered, offered Himself as a hymn of thanksgiving to the Father, and a sacrifice of thanksgiving to Him.

If Jonah offered a sacrifice of thanksgiving to God in the belly of the fish, it was as a type of the Lord Christ, who saw everyone united against Him, and in love fulfilled His vow to the Father by offering His life as a ransom for many, even for His very tormentors!

In Christ Jesus the Sacrifice our whole life is turned into a harp in the hand of the Holy Spirit, singing a symphony of thanksgiving and gratitude to the Father, not with our mouths only but through all our conduct! If Jonah became a psalmist in the belly of the fish, it was to declare what the Lord Christ does in us through His sufferings, for He creates in us a nature of thanksgiving that touches our whole being, instead of the ingratitude that corrupted our life.
“And the LORD spake unto the fish, and it vomited out Jonah upon the dry land.” [10].

St. John Chrysostom holds that God gave Jonah successive lessons in showing gentleness toward others: if the fish swallowed him and then cast him out without harming him, is it not fitting for him to show gentleness toward his brothers in humanity, even if they are Gentiles?! “The waves received him and did not choke him, and the fish caught him without destroying him... So it was fitting for the prophet to be gentle and merciful, and not to be harsher than the beast of prey or the ignorant mariners or the violent waves.

St. Jerome holds that the expression “vomited out” points to the victorious life coming out from where death is, for the belly of hell could not hold our Jonah, nor could corruption touch Him. As the Psalmist says: “For thou wilt not leave my soul in hell; neither wilt thou suffer thine Holy One to see corruption” (Ps 16:10).
He rose from among the dead as the firstfruits for us, raising us with Him. As St. Jerome says: [He who died to free the captives from the bonds of death is able to lead many to life].

1 And the word of the LORD came unto Jonah the second time, saying, 2 "Arise, go unto Nineveh, that great city, and preach unto it the preaching that I bid thee." 3 So Jonah arose, and went unto Nineveh, according to the word of the LORD. Now Nineveh was an exceeding great city of three days' journey. 4 And Jonah began to enter into the city a day's journey, and he cried, and said, "Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown."

Since Jonah had enjoyed life after death, the Lord called him a second time to service, that they too might enjoy life. It is remarkable that God did not rebuke Jonah with a single word, nor wound his feelings because of his flight from the first mission, for the Scripture says:

"And the word of the LORD came unto Jonah the second time, saying, Arise, go unto Nineveh, that great city, and preach unto it the preaching that I bid thee. So Jonah arose, and went unto Nineveh, according to the word of the LORD. Now Nineveh was an exceeding great city of three days' journey. And Jonah began to enter into the city a day's journey, and he cried, and said, Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown" [1-4].

He describes Nineveh in this way: "an exceeding great city of three days' journey." In the literal sense it means that it was a huge city that a man could cross in three days, or that he would keep walking about in its streets for three days. In the spiritual sense, however, Nineveh, as the capital of Assyria, had surrendered itself to Satan and worshipped idols, yet God looks upon it as His great city, which the enemy had seized by its surrendering itself to him. God does not despise His creation, especially man. Even if man turns away from Him, He waits for his salvation and his return to Him, as a great city belonging to Him, in which the Holy Trinity dwells.

In our study of the Book of Joshua we saw that the number 3 refers to faith in the Holy Trinity, as it also refers to the Resurrection on the third day. This is the secret of man's greatness, that he becomes the city of God, or as the Scripture calls it, "a city of truth" (Zech 8:3), the kingdom of the Holy Trinity, bearing witness to the Lord's Resurrection by its life raised up in Him.

Jonah responded to the call and entered the city a day's journey to proclaim repentance. What is this entering but an indication of the appearing of One of the Holy Trinity, God the Word, who became incarnate and suffered, and so became as one who is in our city? He dwelt in our midst as one of us; through Him we received the work of the Holy Trinity, and we obtained salvation!

Jonah cried that after forty days the city of Nineveh would be overthrown, while in the Septuagint it reads: after three days the city of Nineveh will be overthrown. If the number 40 refers to our life in time (which is why the Lord Christ fasted forty days, that we may fast all the days of our life), then Nineveh is overthrown after forty days because heaven and earth pass away so that we may enjoy the new heaven and the new earth. And if the number 3 refers to the Resurrection with the Lord Christ, then the old Nineveh must needs be demolished so that the new one may rise in Him.

entries.section: 2. The faith and repentance of Nineveh:

paragraphs.text: 5 So the people of Nineveh believed God, and proclaimed a fast, and put on sackcloth, from the greatest of them even to the least of them. 6 For word came unto the king of Nineveh, and he arose from his throne, and he laid his robe from him, and covered him with sackcloth, and sat in ashes. 7 And he caused it to be proclaimed and published through Nineveh by the decree of the king and his nobles, saying, "Let neither man nor beast, herd nor flock, taste any thing: let them not feed, nor drink water: 8 But let man and beast be covered with sackcloth, and cry mightily unto God: yea, let them turn every one from his evil way, and from the violence that is in their hands. 9 Who can tell if God will turn and repent, and turn away from his fierce anger, that we perish not?"
"So the people of Nineveh believed God, and proclaimed a fast, and put on sackcloth, from the greatest of them even to the least of them" [5].
St. Jerome says: [Nineveh believed, but Israel resisted in unbelief. The uncircumcised believed, while the circumcised continued in their unbelief.]

The faith of the people of Nineveh was joined to action, so they offered a practical repentance whose weapons were fasting and sackcloth. As St. Jerome says: [Fasting and sackcloth are the weapons of repentance, a help to sinners. Fasting comes first, then sackcloth; the first points to what is unseen and is followed by what is seen. The one stands before the Lord continually, and the other stands for a time before men.] It is as though it befits our repentance to begin with hidden fasting and secret practical life, and only then go forth to outward works.
St. Jerome says: [In repentance sackcloth is joined to fasting, so that the empty belly and the garments of mourning entreat the Lord greatly in prayer.]

All offered practical repentance to God. The great as well as the small put on sackcloth; the king and the nobles led the procession of repentance, and all the people took part in it, and even the beasts... although Jonah had not given a single word of hope, nor spoken to them of God's love and compassion, nor taught them anything about repentance... Nineveh thus became a wonderful and living example of true repentance.

Who is the king who put on sackcloth but the human will, which bows down before God to proclaim its submission to Him and its willingness to become poor for the sake of Him who, being rich, became poor to enrich it? Repentance begins with an inner change in man's will, that is, our inner king. The king took off his royal robe, put on sackcloth and sat in ashes, so that our human will may take off the garments that are the work of its own hands and confess its nakedness and its own poverty. Then the Lord clothes it with His heavenly royal will, grants it the new man who is after His image, raises it from the dunghill to sit with the heavenly ones, and gives the soul a place in the bosom of the Father. As for the nobles, in their repentance they point to the sanctifying of the gifts and abilities we have, that they may work for the kingdom of God. As for the beasts, they point to the body with its energies, which previously walked in darkness in an animal manner. In other words, repentance touches the whole man: his soul and his body, his will and his abilities, his feelings and his conduct!

Here it befits us to realize that what drew God's heart to them was neither their fasting in itself nor the sackcloth in itself, but the repentant heart that fasting supported and sackcloth helped. As St. John Chrysostom says: [The people of Nineveh fasted and gained the love of God, whereas the Jews fasted and profited nothing, but rather received blame (Isa 58:3, 7; 1 Cor 9:26). So the danger in fasting is great for those who do not know how they ought to fast. Let us learn the rules of this discipline, so that we may not run in vain or fight as one that beateth the air, or be, in our sorrow, wrestling with shadows. Fasting is a medicine, but it is not always beneficial if it is used in an improper way through the inexperience of those who use it.]

entries.section: 2. The faith and repentance of Nineveh:

paragraphs.text: What draws our attention in the repentance of the people of Nineveh is their joyful hope. The words of Jonah were few and severe, yet the people of Nineveh did not lose their hope in the merciful Lord. As St. John Chrysostom says: [The message of God on the lips of Jonah was plain; it said nothing about their being received if they returned, yet they proclaimed their repentance, saying: "Who can tell if God will turn and repent, and turn away from his fierce anger, that we perish not?" [9]. If the Gentiles, who did not understand, were able to grasp this, how much more does it befit us, who have been trained in the divine teachings and have seen many examples of this kind throughout history and in our present experience, to grasp it?!]
"And God saw their works, that they turned from their evil way; and God repented of the evil, that he had said that he would do unto them; and he did it not" [10].
Observations on this text:

First: Repentance does not need a long time but a change of heart. The people of Nineveh were able to seize the mercies of God not through the length of time but through the sincerity of their return to God. Although it befits us to spend all our life in continual, unceasing repentance, longing to reach the measure of the stature of the fulness of Christ, this view does not take away from us the awareness of God's mercies, which await the return of every man so as to embrace him at once. St. John Chrysostom says: [Where the fear of God is, there is no need of (many) days nor of the intervention of time; on the contrary, where the fear of God is not, days are of no use... If we cast a rusty vessel into the furnace of the fear of God, it is purified in a short time.]

Second: The word "evil" here means the afflictions or chastenings that God allows to come upon man to discipline him or to be an example for others. They are evil in man's eyes, but they are not so in their nature. As Tertullian says: [The Greeks also sometimes use the word "evils" for "afflictions and the harms that befall"]. Father Theodore has confirmed this as well.

Third: In former times some stumbled at the Scripture's expression "the Lord repented." Does God change His mind? God uses human language to bring the meaning near to us. God does not repent in the sense of changing His mind; rather it is man who changes his position toward God, so that the judgment concerning him becomes different. When man is stubborn he falls under chastening, and when he turns back from his evil and returns to God he finds Him with open arms. This is what we call repentance! When God issues a sentence of chastening, He does not insist on carrying it out; He issues the sentence so that man may turn from his evil and be pardoned.

St. John Chrysostom says in this regard: [In the days of Jonah, had God not threatened destruction, the destruction would not have been removed from them... Had He not threatened us with hell, we would all have fallen into it.] He also says: [The threat of danger causes deliverance from it... The threat of death brings life. The sentence was annulled after it was announced, contrary to what happens among temporal judges, who, once they pass a sentence, it becomes effective... With God, on the contrary, the sentence is announced in order to annul it.]

"1 But it displeased Jonah exceedingly, and he was very angry. 2 And he prayed unto the LORD, and said, I pray thee, O LORD, was not this my saying, when I was yet in my country? Therefore I fled before unto Tarshish: for I knew that thou art a gracious God, and merciful, slow to anger, and of great kindness, and repentest thee of the evil. 3 Therefore now, O LORD, take, I beseech thee, my life from me; for it is better for me to die than to live. 4 Then said the LORD, Doest thou well to be angry?" [1-4].

St. John Chrysostom says: [Truly the prophet was ashamed when he saw that what he had prophesied had not come to pass... But God is not ashamed, seeking one thing only: the salvation of men and the good of His servant.]

St. Jerome holds that Jonah's grief and complaint rest on his perception of God's mercies and compassions, for it was not possible for him to present God to the people of Nineveh as a harsh God. Therefore he longed for death, and could not bear to see God's mercies reach the Gentiles while Israel perished. So he says on the prophet's lips: [I alone among the multitude of the prophets announce to my people their destruction through the salvation of others.] These feelings, full of love toward his people, even if they seemed to carry harshness toward the Gentiles, made him ask God to take his life, for his death was better than his life... Jonah repeats the same request once again after the gourd withered, that is, Israel! In any case, this request or desire carried a prophetic aspect: as a representative of the Lord Christ, or as a type of Him, he asks for death on behalf of his people, looking forward to the salvation of mankind being accomplished by the death of the Cross, not by coming down from it or being delivered from it. It is no wonder, then, that the Lord Christ Himself said to His disciples: "With desire I have desired to eat this passover with you" (Lk 22:15). Since He is the slain Paschal Lamb, He desires to give His life with His own hands, in order to give His believers His Body and Blood, shed for the salvation of the world!

Jonah longed to die, but in bitterness because of the perishing of his people, which was made known through the salvation of the Gentiles. But our true Jonah came for this hour, going forward to the sufferings with joy, despising the shame (Heb 12:2), to redeem all mankind.
"So Jonah went out of the city, and sat on the east side of the city, and there made him a booth, and sat under it in the shadow, till he might see what would become of the city" [5].

Jonah went out of the city, grieved and full of anger, and sat east of the city, watching what the Lord would do to the city. Perhaps Jonah himself represented the Jewish mind, or the elder son who stood outside the house in pain because his younger brother had returned to his father's house (Lk 15:25-31). While the house was full of joy and gladness at the return of the prodigal, the elder son, in his self-righteousness, remained outside the house blaming his father with harsh words.

The rebellious city of Nineveh seized the mercies of God through faith working by love, while the prophet Jonah went out of it to set up a booth that was the work of his own hands, that is, his self-righteousness, counting himself better than others and awaiting God's wrath upon them.

"6 And the LORD God prepared a gourd, and made it to come up over Jonah, that it might be a shadow over his head, to deliver him from his grief. So Jonah was exceeding glad of the gourd. 7 But God prepared a worm when the morning rose the next day, and it smote the gourd that it withered. 8 And it came to pass, when the sun did arise, that God prepared a vehement east wind; and the sun beat upon the head of Jonah, that he fainted, and wished in himself to die, and said, It is better for me to die than to live" [6-8].
What did God intend by this gourd, which the Lord God prepared and then prepared a worm to smite it?

First: Without doubt the gourd is the Jewish people, of whom the Lord said: "Thou hast had pity on the gourd, for the which thou hast not laboured, neither madest it grow; which came up in a night, and perished in a night" [10].

Jonah was exceeding glad of the gourd [6], for he greatly loved his people, but he had no merit in this gourd... He did not plant it, nor tend it, nor watch over it. It was God who raised up Israel and tended him, brought him out of the bondage of Pharaoh, gave him the Law, brought him into the Promised Land and gave him the prophecies, and did not leave him in need of anything. As the Lord rebuked him, saying: "And now, O inhabitants of Jerusalem, and men of Judah, judge, I pray you, betwixt me and my vineyard. What could have been done more to my vineyard, that I have not done in it?" (Isa 5:3-4).

It befitted Jonah, who represents a small part of one of the branches of this gourd, not to be grieved and angry, for the One who raised up the gourd, chose it and tended it is God Himself, who sent him to Nineveh to shepherd it also through him!

He called it "which came up in a night, and perished in a night" [10]. It was not a "son of the day" or a "son of light," but a "son of a night," because it rejected its Savior, the Sun of Righteousness, and loved darkness rather than light. As St. John the Evangelist says: "That was the true Light, which lighteth every man that cometh into the world... He came unto his own, and his own received him not. But as many as received him, to them gave he power to become the sons of God, even to them that believe on his name" (Jn 1:9-12).

Second: God raised up a gourd for Jonah to draw him away from his booth, which was the work of his own hands, as though He were drawing man away from his self-righteousness so that he might enjoy a shade that is from the hand of God, his Creator and Shepherd. But the gourd had to wither, so that in place of this weak plant there might be raised up the wood of the Cross, under which the Church takes shelter to enjoy the joy of the Gospel, saying: "I sat down under his shadow with great delight, and his fruit was sweet to my taste" (Song 2:3).

If Jonah went out to the east of the city, awaiting in the spirit of prophecy the rising of the Sun of Righteousness (Mal 4:2), who shines not on Israel alone but on all the Gentiles, then he was exceedingly glad of the gourd because Israel enjoyed the Law and the prophecies to lead him to his Savior. But he was not able to accept Israel's fall as the way for faith to go forth to the Gentiles, and so he was grieved over the withered gourd. He wanted to live under the types and among the shadows of the prophecies as a refuge for himself, and did not realize that they are the way that carries him to the Desire of all nations.
If the Law is our schoolmaster to bring us to Christ, as the Apostle Paul says, yet Israel clung to the letter of the Law and the formalities of worship, rejecting the life-giving wood of the Cross.

I say: let our souls go forth to the east to enjoy the shining of the Lord upon them; let the gourd of the killing letter wither, that we may enjoy the life-giving Spirit, and receive within us the Desire of all nations as the secret of our enlightenment, our joy and our people!

Third: Just as God had spoken to Jonah before through the raging tempest, the tossed ship, the Gentile sailors, the lot and the whale, He now speaks to him through the weak gourd, the east wind and the worm that destroyed the gourd. God speaks at every stage in the language to which man responds and which he understands. When Jonah was in revolt in his heart against God's decision concerning Nineveh, having made the decision to flee, God spoke to him in the language of violence that befits a violent heart. He spoke to him in the language of the tempest so that he might realize his inner turmoil, and in the language of the Gentile sailors so that he might realize that he had gone lame from the spirit of faith. He spoke to him through the ship tossed by the winds so that he might discover his heart, which was about to drift in the midst of the sea of this world, and He spoke with him through the whale so that he might realize the abyss into which he had been swept, the depths that swallowed him, and the prison in which he had placed himself... And now, when Jonah came out frail, with no strength to resist, He spoke to him through the gourd, a weak plant, and the corrupting worm, so that he might realize that he is only a weak plant destroyed by the worm of ingratitude and non-submission.
In short, we say that by the language in which the Lord speaks to us we discover our hidden depths.

Fourth: St. Hippolytus of Rome sees that the hot east wind which God prepared refers to the Antichrist, who comes out of the east by divine permission to oppose the Church shortly before the Lord's final coming.

9 And God said to Jonah, "Doest thou well to be angry for the gourd?" And he said, "I do well to be angry, even unto death." 10 Then said the LORD, "Thou hast had pity on the gourd, for the which thou hast not laboured, neither madest it grow; which came up in a night, and perished in a night: 11 And should not I spare Nineveh, that great city, wherein are more than sixscore thousand persons that cannot discern between their right hand and their left hand; and also much cattle?"

God concluded His dialogue with Jonah with this beautiful statement: "Thou hast had pity on the gourd, for the which thou hast not laboured, neither madest it grow; which came up in a night, and perished in a night: And should not I spare Nineveh, that great city, wherein are more than sixscore thousand persons that cannot discern between their right hand and their left hand; and also much cattle?" [10-11].
In this way God reveals His love for mankind, who are the work of His hands.
Nineveh, as St. Jerome says, is: [the great city, which is the Church, containing the twelve spiritual tribes who return to childhood in its innocence and simplicity.]
